exercises.title: Checking Several Types at Once
description: Assign four variables — one each of type int,
float, str, and bool — and
print all four of their types with a single
print() call, separated by spaces.
<pre>> python program.py
<class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'str'> <class 'bool'>
Just like you've done before, handing print() multiple
values separated by commas puts a space between each one
automatically — that works just as well with type()
calls as it does with plain values.

exercises.title: Reassigning a Variable's Type
description: Assign an integer to a variable and print its type. Then
reassign that same variable to a piece of text, and
print its type again — both on the same line, separated by a
space.
<pre>> python program.py
<class 'int'> <class 'str'>
In Python, a variable isn't locked to one type forever — the
same name can be reassigned to hold a completely different kind of
value later in the program. Use print(..., end=" ") on
the first print so the second one lands on the same line instead of a
new one.

exercises.title: Fix the Bug: Missing Quotes
description: This code is supposed to assign the text blue to a
variable and print its type. Run it and see what actually happens.
Text needs to be wrapped in quotes. Without them, Python doesn't see
blue as a piece of text at all — it looks for a
variable named blue, and since none exists, the
program crashes.

exercises.title: Fix the Bug: Double Equals
description: This code is supposed to assign the number 100 to a
variable and print its type. Run it and see what actually happens.
= and == do very different jobs in Python.
A single = assigns a value to a variable. A double
== compares two values and produces
True or False — it never creates a
variable at all.

exercises.title: Fix the Bug: Lowercase Boolean
description: This code is supposed to assign a boolean value to a variable and
print its type. Run it and see what actually happens.
Python's boolean values are True and False
— both capitalized. Lowercase true isn't a boolean at
all as far as Python is concerned; it looks like a reference to a
variable called true, which doesn't exist.
